title: Loftus and Palmer (1974) Knowledge Base
summary: Atomic knowledge extraction covering Loftus and Palmer's (1974) study on reconstructive memory, including aims, design, procedures, results, conclusions, strengths, limitations, and counter-evidence.

knowledge.text: Study: Loftus and Palmer (1974) - 'Reconstruction of automobile destruction'.
Aim: To investigate whether leading questions affect estimates of speed and memory of an event (reconstructive memory / schema theory).
Experiment 1 sample: 45 American students.
Experiment 1 design: Independent measures design.
Experiment 1 procedure: Participants watched 7 film clips of traffic accidents.
Experiment 1 critical question: 'About how fast were the cars going when they ___ each other?'
Experiment 1 Independent Variable (IV): The critical verb used in the question ('smashed', 'collided', 'bumped', 'hit', 'contacted').
Experiment 1 Dependent Variable (DV): Speed estimate in miles per hour (mph).
Experiment 1 result: The mean speed estimate for 'smashed' was 40.8 mph.
Experiment 1 result: The mean speed estimate for 'collided' was 39.3 mph.
Experiment 1 result: The mean speed estimate for 'bumped' was 38.1 mph.
Experiment 1 result: The mean speed estimate for 'hit' was 34.0 mph.
Experiment 1 result: The mean speed estimate for 'contacted' was 31.8 mph.
Experiment 2 sample: 150 students.
Experiment 2 procedure: Participants watched a 1-minute film of a multiple car crash.
Experiment 2 groups: 50 participants were asked a speed question with 'smashed', 50 with 'hit', and 50 served as a control receiving no speed question.
Experiment 2 procedure: One week later, participants were asked 'Did you see any broken glass?'.
Experiment 2 fact: There was no broken glass in the accident film clip.
Experiment 2 result: 16 participants (32%) in the 'smashed' condition reported seeing broken glass.
Experiment 2 result: 7 participants (14%) in the 'hit' condition reported seeing broken glass.
Experiment 2 result: 6 participants (12%) in the control condition reported seeing broken glass.
Conclusion: Leading questions can distort memory.
Conclusion: Post-event information is integrated into the memory of the event, demonstrating that memory is reconstructive.
Strength: It was a laboratory experiment with high control and a standardised procedure, allowing cause-and-effect to be established.
Strength: The study has been replicated.
Limitation: The sample of students is not representative of all age groups or drivers.
Limitation: Watching film clips lacks the emotional arousal of real accidents, resulting in low ecological validity.
Limitation: Demand characteristics were possible.
Counter-evidence: Yuille and Cutshall (1986) found real witnesses of a shooting were accurate despite misleading questions.

intro.text: You are investigating whether leading questions alter speed estimates and reconstruct memories.
45 students in an independent measures design watch seven traffic accident film clips.
You test critical verbs like smashed or hit and measure speed estimates in mph.
150 students watch a crash film. One week later, you ask about broken glass.
Post-event information integrates into memories, proving human memory is reconstructive.
